Today I want to look at an increasingly common feature of modern cities: vertical farming.
Vertical farms grow crops in stacked layers, often indoors, using far less land than traditional agriculture.
Most systems rely on hydroponics, a method of growing plants in nutrient-rich water rather than soil.
Compared to traditional farming, vertical farms can use up to ninety-five percent less water.
This matters increasingly as cities grow, since it's estimated that around seventy percent of the world's population will live in urban areas by 2050.

One of the biggest obstacles to wider adoption has consistently been the high upfront cost of the lighting and climate-control systems required, which remains far more limiting than any issue with the crops themselves.

lines.text: Despite that, Singapore has emerged as something of a global leader in this space, largely because the government has directly subsidised vertical farm construction as part of a broader food security strategy.

One well-known example is a facility called Sky Greens, which was among the first commercial vertical farms in Asia.
It primarily grows leafy vegetables, which tend to suit vertical systems better than root crops.
The facility uses rotating towers, which slowly turn the crops toward light throughout the day to maximise growth.
Researchers there are now exploring whether similar systems could eventually be adapted for use in disaster relief settings, where fresh food access is often extremely limited.
Next week, we'll examine the economics of vertical farming in more detail. Thank you.
